cur:monumental-san-venanzio-apse-christ.summary: In the clouds at the top of the apse, a bust of Christ with long dark hair and beard raises his hand in blessing, flanked by two angels who emerge from the streaked red and blue sky. Below him (not shown here) stands the Virgin in prayer among apostles and Dalmatian martyrs whose relics were brought to Rome.
facts: Pope John IV (640–642), a native of Dalmatia, brought relics of Dalmatian saints to Rome and built an oratory in their honour, decorated with mosaics that include his own portrait holding a model of the building.

cur:monumental-san-venanzio-apse-christ.notes: Commons file names call the chapel 'cappella di s. teodoro' and date the mosaic 'c. 650'; the usual name is the Chapel of San Venanzio.

cur:objects2-vam-printed-linen-issue-of-.summary: A large, faded linen from Akhmim in Upper Egypt carries several biblical scenes in dyed outline, separated by bands of discs and blossoms. The museum identifies Moses receiving the Law and, in the lower left, the woman with the issue of blood reaching out to touch the robe of Christ. Though the figures are now hard to read, the cloth is a rare early example of Gospel miracles depicted on a domestic textile.
facts: Akhmim (ancient Panopolis) was one of the great sources of late Roman and Coptic textiles preserved in Egyptian burials.
The V&A acquired the piece in 1897 (museum number 722-1897).
cur:objects2-vam-printed-linen-issue-of-.notes: Christ's figure is very faint in the photograph; identification rests on the museum's description.

cur:objects2-walters-koimesis-ivory.summary: The Virgin lies on her deathbed among the mourning apostles, while Christ stands behind the bier and receives her swaddled, child-like soul; two angels descend with veiled hands to carry it to heaven. As the museum notes, Saint Peter swings a censer at the left and Saint Paul, at the right, bends to kiss the Virgin's feet.
facts: The Greek name of the feast, Koimesis, means 'falling asleep'.
Before entering the Walters collection in 1927 the plaque passed through the hands of the Berlin dealer Paul Cassirer and the Paris dealer Henri Daguerre.

walters:54.2575.summary: This squat bronze censer is cast all round with crowded scenes in relief, separated by palm-like trees, and a band of leafy scrolls runs round the rim. The Walters identifies the Annunciation, Nativity, Crucifixion and the Women at the Tomb on the sides, while on the underside the Virgin sits enthroned holding the Christ Child. Swung in the liturgy, it wrapped the story of Christ's life, death and resurrection in clouds of incense.
facts: The Walters explains that incense, blessed and burned on coals inside such censers, was believed to carry prayers up to heaven, and that its ingredients such as frankincense, myrrh and aloeswood were thought to purify.
The Walters attributes the censer to Syria and dates it to the 7th–8th century.
It was given to the museum in 1981 by Mrs Carol L. Brewster.
walters:54.2575.notes: The museum's culture field reads 'Eastern Orthodox'; style set to Byzantine, following the museum's description of it as a Byzantine censer.
